newsitem.title: PERU: Peruvians cheer end of siege, doubt Fujimori boost.
newsitem.headline: Peruvians cheer end of siege, doubt Fujimori boost.

text.p: Peruvians rejoiced on Wednesday at the spectacular hostage rescue at the Japanese ambassador's residence but some doubted President Alberto Fujimori's plunging popularity would get a significant boost.

"As a politician his image has fallen quite a lot and this could raise it a bit but I don't think it will raise it as much as the president thinks," Asuncion Chavez, a singer with a tropical music band, said.

Opinion polls released last weekend showed Fujimori's approval ratings had plunged to near historic lows with his government mired in fruitless negotiations to free the 72 hostages and a series of scandals in the armed forces.

He reinforced his reputation as a political strongman when he ordered the surprise assault on Tuesday on the mined and booby-trapped compound where 14 Tupac Amaru Revolutionary (MRTA) guerrillas had held 72 VIPs under the gun for 126 days.

Until then, most Peruvians surveyed in polls called for a negotiated solution to Latin America's longest hostage siege. But months of painstaking talks between Fujimori and the guerrillas on freeing the hostages brought only glimpses of progress, giving the Peruvian leader little choice but to strike, beer saleswoman Regina Munoz said.
"There were lots of talks and nothing concrete. He had to act," Munoz said. "While we regret the loss of life, Fujimori had no choice in the end."

One captive, a local judge, died and two were seriously injured in the fierce gun battle along with two of the crack troops and all 14 of the jungle-trained rebels. The guerrilla takeover of Japanese Ambassador Morihisa Aoki's home during a cocktail party on Dec 17. had proved the toughest challenge of Fujimori's seven years in office.
Although all the rebels and their leader Nestor Cerpa were killed, this may not be the body blow that will finally smash the Cuban-inspired movement, taxi driver Victor Montalba said.
"If the government says terrorism is over, that's wrong," he said. "The group's numbers have been reduced but there are still members and we cannot afford to lower our guard."

Some 200 MRTA fighters are still believed to be training in the jungles of central Peru. But for many Peruvians the headline-grabbing siege was just a temporary distraction from the country's economic problems and they hoped Fujimori would now turn his attention to tackling the high level of poverty.
"We are proud of the military action but if Fujimori really wants to improve his reputation he must change his policies towards the poor," Chavez said.
If Peru succeeds in shedding its violent reputation, this will help improve the lives of ordinary people who are tired of more than a decade of guerrilla warfare.

"On an economic level there could be other countries which now give us a little more support," waiter Luis Galan said. "After suffering so much terrorism, the best would be to live in a quiet country," he said.

But for now the nightmare that hung over Peru throughout Christmas, New Years and Easter has ended and Peruvians' main feeling is one of relief. "I feel like I am the one who has been freed," taxi driver Juan Behar said.
